title: Borrowed words, Indonesian rules
goal: Recognise and build the international words Indonesian has borrowed (*-wan, -isme, -is, -si, -tas*), spell them the Indonesian way, and stop trusting the ones that only look familiar.
bekal: turn roots into people with *-wan* and *-wati*: *wisatawan, wartawan, karyawati*
spell loanwords by the rules: *kualitas, organisasi, praktis, aktivitas*
avoid classic false friends such as *aktual, pesimis, travel* and *kantor*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Gladi presentasi Yoga
dialogs.intro: A Thursday afternoon in July at the balai desa in Sumberwangi. Yoga is rehearsing the presentation he will give Pak Harun next week. Sarah and Bu Ratna are his audience, and they are not easy to impress.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Oke, jadi basically target market kita itu wisatawan Gen Z yang concern sama sustainability.
lines.id: OK, so basically our target market is Gen Z tourists who care about sustainability.
lines.literal: OK, so basically target market we that tourist Gen Z who concern with sustainability.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Mas Yoga, pelan-pelan. Target market itu apa? Saya cuma nangkep “kita”.
lines.id: Slow down, Yoga. What's a target market? The only word I caught was “our”.
lines.literal: Mas Yoga, slow-slow. target market that what? I only catch “we”.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Maaf, Bu. Maksudnya pasar sasaran: wisatawan muda yang peduli lingkungan.
lines.id: Sorry. I mean the market we're aiming at: young tourists who care about the environment.
lines.literal: sorry, Mrs. meaning-its market target: tourist young who care environment.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah, itu jauh lebih jelas. Pak Harun juga pasti langsung paham.
lines.id: There you go, that's much clearer. Pak Harun will get it straight away too.
lines.literal: there, that far more clear. Mr Harun also surely straight-away understand.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Tapi kalau pakai istilah Inggris, kesannya lebih profesional, Mbak.
lines.id: But English terms make it sound more professional.
lines.literal: but if use term English, impression-its more professional, Miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Lucunya, “profesional” itu sendiri kata serapan, dan sudah jadi bahasa Indonesia.
lines.id: The funny thing is, “profesional” is a loanword itself, and it's already Indonesian.
lines.literal: funny-the, “professional” that itself word absorbed, and already become language Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Lagi pula, ibu-ibu homestay nggak semuanya ngerti bahasa Inggris, lho.
lines.id: Besides, not all the homestay ladies understand English, you know.
lines.literal: besides, mothers homestay not all-of-them understand language English, [lho].

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Siap, Bu. Slide berikutnya: kita perlu improve kualitas pelayanan.
lines.id: Yes, ma'am. Next slide: we need to improve the quality of service.
lines.literal: ready, Mrs. slide next: we need improve quality service.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Meningkatkan kualitas pelayanan. Kata bendanya boleh serapan, kata kerjanya pakai bahasa Indonesia.
lines.id: *Meningkatkan* the quality of service. The noun can be borrowed, but use an Indonesian verb.
lines.literal: raise quality service. word thing-the may absorbed, word work-the use language Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Oke. Kami juga mau mengundang seniman dan budayawan lokal.
lines.id: OK. We also want to invite local artists and cultural figures.
lines.literal: OK. we also want invite artist and culture-person local.

lines.text: Budayawan? Maksudnya Pak Sastro, dalang itu? Wah, beliau pasti bangga disebut begitu.
lines.id: Cultural figures? You mean Pak Sastro, the puppeteer? He'll be so proud to be called that.
lines.literal: culture-person? meaning-its Mr Sastro, puppet-master that? wow, he surely proud is-called like-that.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Intinya, desa wisata ini bentuk perlawanan terhadap konsumerisme dan pariwisata massal.
lines.id: The point is, this tourist village is a form of resistance to consumerism and mass tourism.
lines.literal: core-its, village tourism this form resistance towards consumerism and tourism mass.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Konsumerisme itu yang belanja terus sampai lupa bayar arisan, ya?
lines.id: Consumerism is when you keep shopping until you forget to pay your arisan, right?
lines.literal: consumerism that which shop continuously until forget pay arisan, [ya]?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Kurang lebih begitu, Bu. Tapi jujur, saya agak pesimis Pak Harun bakal suka.
lines.id: More or less, yes. But honestly, I'm a bit pessimistic that Pak Harun will like it.
lines.literal: less more like-that, Mrs. but honest, I rather pessimistic Mr Harun will like.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Jangan pesimis. Idemu praktis dan kuat; tinggal bahasanya dirapikan.
lines.id: Don't be pessimistic. Your ideas are practical and strong; the language just needs tidying up.
lines.literal: don't pessimistic. idea-your practical and strong; remain language-the is-tidied.

notes: **Basically, concern, sustainability.** Sprinkling English through Indonesian (*campur kode*, code-mixing) is normal among young urban Indonesians, and the Jakarta variety is jokingly called *bahasa Jaksel* after South Jakarta. It is fine with friends. In a village meeting it shuts people out, which is exactly Bu Ratna's point.

**Nangkep, ngerti.** Spoken forms of *menangkap* (to catch) and *mengerti* (to understand). *Nangkep* with a Javanese-style *e* is what you hear in Central Java; in Jakarta it is *nangkap*. “To catch” meaning “to understand” works just as in English: *Saya nggak nangkep maksudnya* — I didn't catch what he meant.

**Pasar sasaran.** For most English terms, Indonesian has an official equivalent (*padanan*), published by the language agency, Badan Bahasa. Some won outright — *daring* (online), *unduh* (download), *unggah* (upload) — and some never did: nobody says *tetikus* for a computer mouse. In formal writing, always try the *padanan* first.

**Budayawan** is a respected person of culture: a writer, thinker or artist whom the public treats as a voice on culture. The suffix *-wan* makes “a person of X”, and it carries prestige, which is why Bu Ratna knows Pak Sastro will be delighted. A *dalang* is the puppet master of the *wayang kulit* shadow play.

**Lagi pula … lho.** *Lagi pula* (also written *lagipula* in chat, but two words in standard spelling) adds one more reason: “besides, anyway”. The *lho* at the end draws attention to something the listener should have noticed — here, gently telling Yoga off.

**Pesimis, bakal.** ⚠️ In everyday Indonesian *pesimis* works as an adjective: *saya pesimis* = I'm pessimistic, not “I am a pessimist”. The same goes for *optimis*. Strictly, KBBI lists *pesimis* as the person and *pesimistis* as the adjective, so careful writing prefers *saya pesimistis*. *Bakal* is the everyday word for *akan* (will); in writing, use *akan*.

grammars.title: -wan and -wati: people defined by what they do
body: These two Sanskrit suffixes attach to a noun to make a person connected with it: *-wan* for a man (or anyone), *-wati* for a woman.
after: Notice *seniman*: after *i*, the suffix often becomes *-man*. *Ilmuwan*, however, keeps *-wan*. Learn these as whole words rather than by rule.

The female forms are slowly fading. Most newspapers now write *wartawan* for any journalist, but *karyawati* and *olahragawati* are still common. *Relawan* (volunteer, from *rela*, willing) has no female form at all.

grammars.title: -isme, -is, -if, -al: the international set
body: Most English words ending in *-ism, -ist, -ic, -ive* and *-al* enter Indonesian with a predictable ending. Once you know the pattern, you can often guess the word — and then check it in the KBBI.
after: ⚠️ *-is* does two jobs: a person (*turis*, *aktivis*) and an adjective (*praktis*, and in speech *pesimis*). Context always tells you which.
⚠️ *Ekonomi* is the economy; *ekonomis* means economical, cheap to run: *Motor ini ekonomis*. The same pair exists for *politik* (politics) and *politis* (political in nature).

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Glosarium Bu Lestari
dialogs.intro: The following Monday, at Dr. Lestari's office at UGM. She has prepared a glossary for the project's mid-year report, and Sarah has questions.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Saya sudah menyusun glosarium kecil untuk laporan kita. Silakan dilihat, Mbak.
lines.id: I've put together a small glossary for our report. Please have a look.
lines.literal: I already compile glossary small for report we. please is-looked-at, Miss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, Bu. Kenapa “sustainability” jadi “keberlanjutan”, bukan “sustainabilitas”?
lines.id: Thank you. Why is “sustainability” *keberlanjutan*, and not *sustainabilitas*?
lines.literal: thank you, Mrs. why “sustainability” become “continuation”, not “sustainabilitas”?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Karena kita sudah punya padanan yang tepat. Serapan baru dipakai kalau padanannya belum ada.
lines.id: Because we already have an exact equivalent. A loanword is only used when there isn't one.
lines.literal: because we already have equivalent which exact. absorbed-word only is-used if equivalent-its not-yet exist.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tapi “kualitas” dan “organisasi” tetap serapan, ya?
lines.id: But *kualitas* and *organisasi* are still loanwords, aren't they?
lines.literal: but “quality” and “organisation” remain absorbed-word, [ya]?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Betul. Ejaannya mengikuti kaidah: “q” menjadi “k”, “-ty” menjadi “-tas”, “-tion” menjadi “-si”.
lines.id: Right. Their spelling follows the rules: *q* becomes *k*, *-ty* becomes *-tas*, *-tion* becomes *-si*.
lines.literal: correct. spelling-its follow rule: “q” become “k”, “-ty” become “-tas”, “-tion” become “-si”.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Berarti “kwalitas” salah? Yoga juga menulis “aktifitas” dengan “f”.
lines.id: So *kwalitas* is wrong? And Yoga wrote *aktifitas* with an *f*.
lines.literal: means “kwalitas” wrong? Yoga also write “aktifitas” with “f”.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Dua-duanya salah. Yang baku “aktivitas” dengan “v”, walaupun “aktif” ditulis dengan “f”.
lines.id: Both are wrong. The standard form is *aktivitas* with a *v*, even though *aktif* is written with an *f*.
lines.literal: two-both wrong. which standard “activity” with “v”, although “active” is-written with “f”.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Ternyata bahasa Indonesia punya jebakan juga, ya.
lines.id: So Indonesian has its traps too.
lines.literal: turns-out language Indonesia have trap also, [ya].

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Satu lagi: “aktual” artinya terkini, bukan “actual”. Berita aktual itu berita terbaru.
lines.id: One more: *aktual* means current, not “actual”. *Berita aktual* is the latest news.
lines.literal: one more: “aktual” meaning-its most-recent, not “actual”. news aktual that news newest.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Wah, saya kira sama dengan “sebenarnya”. Untung Ibu memberi tahu.
lines.id: Oh, I thought it meant *sebenarnya*. Lucky you told me.
lines.literal: wow, I think same with “actually”. luck Mrs give know.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Silakan dibagikan juga ke Yoga. Presentasinya pasti jadi lebih rapi.
lines.id: Do share it with Yoga too. His presentation will be much tidier for it.
lines.literal: please is-shared also to Yoga. presentation-his surely become more tidy.

notes: **Silakan dilihat, silakan dibagikan.** *Silakan* + passive verb is the polite, slightly academic way to invite someone to do something: “it may be looked at”. It sounds more courteous than *Silakan lihat*, and it is how lecturers, officials and receptionists talk.

**Keberlanjutan** is built entirely from Indonesian parts: *lanjut* (continue) → *berlanjut* (to continue) → *ke-…-an* (the state of it), the abstract-noun pattern from Unit 4. Dr. Lestari prefers it for the same reason Sarah told Yoga to say *pasar sasaran*: a native word everyone can parse beats a foreign one.

**Kaidah** is “rule, norm”, especially in grammar and spelling: *kaidah bahasa*, *kaidah ejaan*. The current rulebook is the *EYD* (Ejaan yang Disempurnakan), fifth edition 2022. Dr. Lestari quotes it the way an English teacher quotes Fowler.

**Aktif → aktivitas.** ⚠️ The adjective ends in *-if*, but the noun goes back to *-iv-*: *aktif, aktivitas*; *kreatif, kreativitas*; *produktif, produktivitas*. Many Indonesians write *aktifitas*, and it is one of the errors editors correct most often.

**Aktual** is a false friend. In Indonesian it means current, topical, in the news: *isu aktual* (a current issue). For English “actual” use *sebenarnya* or *yang sesungguhnya*: *biaya yang sebenarnya* (the actual cost).

**Untung Ibu memberi tahu.** *Untung* (profit) at the start of a sentence means “luckily, it's a good thing that”. ⚠️ *Memberi tahu* (to tell, to inform) is written as two words, but its noun is one: *pemberitahuan* (notice, announcement).

grammars.title: Spelling a loanword the Indonesian way
body: Indonesian spells by sound, so a borrowed word is respelled until it looks the way it is pronounced. These are the rules you will meet most often.
after: ⚠️ In each pair, the first is standard and the second is common but wrong: *analisis/analisa, praktik/praktek, kualitas/kwalitas, sistem/sistim, apotek/apotik*. You will see the wrong ones on shop signs every day.
Words that entered through Dutch sometimes keep a Dutch shape: *apotek* (apotheek), *kantor* (kantoor), *wortel* (carrot). The spelling rules still apply; only the source is different.

blocks.text: These words look like English (or Dutch) and mean something else. They cause more misunderstandings than any grammar point in this book, because you do not know you have misunderstood.

head: Indonesian
You might guess
It actually means
rows: a rogue individual in an institution: *oknum polisi*

blocks.text: *Travel* deserves a word: *naik travel ke Semarang* means taking a shared minibus that picks you up at home. And *oknum* is the polite newspaper way to blame one bad apple without blaming the whole barrel.
Indonesian is a Malay language that has borrowed from everyone who ever traded, ruled or preached in the archipelago. The layers are still visible, and knowing them makes new words easier to guess.

blocks.title: Home-made words for new things
items: *surel* (*surat elektronik*) email — official, though most people still say *email*
*warganet* netizen, *swafoto* selfie — the second is used mostly by journalists
